Q: How to set Gitlab pipeline variables with workflow rules A:

You are never going to get the behaviour you want.

The only thing you can do is setup the defaults, and be explicit about each condition as there is not going to be any further processing.

In your case you could just structure it like this.

variables:
  VAR: "no_value"

workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH != $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH && $VAR == "no_value"
      variables:
        VAR: "LAB"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      variables:
        VAR: "DTAP"
    - when: always

job:
  script: 
    - |
      echo "VAR : $VAR"

Of course, if the intention is to change "VAR" even if an upstream pipeline does set it, thats not going to work. Upstream pipeline variables have the most precedence and will override any attempt to set a variable in the downstream.

If you want to have more control, use GitLabs new input variables instead:

spec:
  inputs:
    var:
      default: "no-value"
      description: "some awsome variable"
---
variables:
  VAR: $[[ inputs.var ]] 

workflow:
  ...

And passing values is easy. from your upstream trigger, or include, clause:

include:
- local: ./gitlab/somefile.yaml # or component / project etc
  inputs:
    var: "some-value"

Q: How to parse fuzzy text descriptions into structured time-series data in Python? A:

You can ask most LLMs for structured output. For example, OpenAI, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude... And e.g. if you are using Huggingface models with transformers, you can use a library like lm-format-enforcer. With this, you can restrict the model by providing a schema like:

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Extraction(BaseModel):
    year: int = Field(ge=1900, le=2100)
    platform: str
    subscribers_min: int
    subscribers_max: int
    confidence: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]

and thus force the LLM to only give you compliant answers. If you are expecting multiple extractions in a single answer, just ask for list[Extraction]. No need to parse anything.

Q: Is there such a thing as short-circuit evaluation within a regular expression? If so, how to write it? A:

Is there a way to write the regular expression such that it captures nothing and stops searching at the first match?

That's what it does by default. You have to use the -all switch to make it search for all the matches and return the number found. Without this, it simply returns 1 as soon as it finds a match.

Regarding some of the other issues you raised, you can use (?:...) to create a non-capturing group. You can also use [[,] to match a square bracket or comma, rather than alternation \[|, in a group. Or use [[:<:]] and [[:>:]] to match the beginning and end of a word, respectively, rather than matching the punctuation characters explicitly. So the regexp could be

[[:<:]](?:$rnodes)[[:>:]]

Q: An implementation of the Jaro Winkler distance algorithm in Transact SQL A:

How can you implement it?

There are a range of ways you could implement Jaro Winkler in T-SQL, and when writing this answer, Microsoft have started previewing a built-in function for it in SQL 17.x, but given that the built-in version isn't yet production-ready and many people don't have bleeding-edge SQL Server instances, plus the fact that all of the implementations I could find, regardless of whether they had the logic correct, had major performance issues that made them impossible to scale - namely the use of lots of procedural loops that SQL is just not great at managing, I've decided to put my implementation in here as a decently scalable solution.

How can you make it performant?

Ultimately it may well be most performant to create a CLR function so you can run the logic in a language that's better suited to the greedy-matching process that Jaro Winkler requires, but that's a whole other security concern that may make it unavailable to many. So my concerns here become:

  • Use exclusively T-SQL, and lean towards more legacy functions, especially considering that a built-in function may soon be available to those with the newest version

  • Optimise for performance

    • An inline TVF will allow us to CROSS APPLY for scalable application and let the query optimiser work well, meaning we need a single-statement solution - no procedural loops.

    • Avoid recursive CTEs as well wherever possible, and limit recursions if they can't be avoided (they can't.)

    • Use the cheapest built in functions possible (without making it totally unreadable).

How did I implement it?

It's super-unreadable to just put everything into one big query with subqueries condensed and collapsed to the max, so I've used CTEs to break it down into logical steps. Broadly:

  1. Get the lengths of the longest and shortest strings, and use them to calculate the size of the window in a single-row CTE.

  2. Generate a CTE for each string with a row for each of its characters, along with indexes.

  3. Join these CTEs on character equality within the calculated window size, giving us every possible match candidate for each character of each string.

  4. Use a recursive CTE to pick one match for each matchable character from string 1 (in ascending order), ensuring the earliest unused match from string 2 is applied each time.

    • I used a bitmask with a flipped bit corresponding to the character's position in its string to allow cheap bitwise operations keeping track of which characters from string 2 had already been matched to a specific string 1 character.

    • I used a CROSS APPLIED subquery to SELECT all the match candidates for higher-indexed string 1 characters (unmatched due to order) and unmatched string 2 characters (unmatched filtered by the bit mask).

    • I included a ROW_NUMBER() in the subquery so that I could pick only one match per recursion.

  5. Re-index the list of qualified matched characters so we can see which characters match out of order.

    • Because we made sure to match each character exactly once (in step 4) there will be an even number of out-of-order characters.

    • Jaro counts the number of times we need to swap these out-of-order matches to get them in the same order, so it's half the count of matches.

  6. Find the earliest mismatched character out of the first four of each string, telling you how long the matching prefix is. This is another single-row CTE.

  7. For readability I pulled out the variables from each first so that the equations would be easier to parse.

ALTER FUNCTION [dbo].[tvfJaroWinkler](
    @String1 varchar(64), 
    @String2 varchar(64)
)
RETURNS TABLE
AS RETURN
WITH cteStringVariables AS (
    --Get a row that can be used in below SELECTs exposing string lengths and calculating window size
    SELECT 
        CAST(MAX(L.[L]) AS float) [MaxLen], --MaxLen/MinLen can stand in for the two string lengths in the Jaro
        CAST(MIN(L.[L]) AS float) [MinLen], --calculation because Jaro treats the two lengths symmetrically.
        ISNULL(NULLIF(FLOOR(MAX(L.[L])/2)-1,-1),0) [Window]  --The distance forward or backward we can look for a match.
    FROM (VALUES
        (LEN(@String1),1),
        (LEN(@String2),2)
    ) L(L, S)
), cteString1 AS (
    --Use a numbers table to return a row for each character in string 1, along with its index.
    SELECT
        N.[Number] [Ix],
        SUBSTRING(@String1,N.[Number],1) [Chr]
    FROM master.dbo.GetNumbers() N
    WHERE N.[Number] <= IIF(@String1=@String2,0,LEN(@String1)) --IIF() stops us generating any rows for a perfect match so we save the cpu cycles
), cteString2 AS (
    --Use a numbers table to return a row for each character in string 2, along with its index.
    SELECT
        N.[Number] [Ix],
        B.[IxBitMask], --We'll use this to track which characters from @String2 have already been selected in our recursive cte below
        SUBSTRING(@String2,N.[Number],1) [Chr]
    FROM master.dbo.GetNumbers() N
    --Generate a bit mask for each S2.Ix so we can do cheap checks for whether each character has been used in a match in cteGreedy below.
    CROSS APPLY (
        SELECT
            POWER(
                CONVERT(    --The first argument of POWER() determines the output type and bitwise operations require integer types. 
                    bigint, --Using bigint gives us the maximum (64) bits to assign to Ix2s, allowing us to track whether they've been used.
                    IIF(
                        N.[Number]=64, --Bigint's most significant bit stores the *sign*, so it's range is -2^63 to 2^63-1. 2^63 is out of range.
                        -2,            --If we want that 64th bit in our mask, we need to flip it by manually shifting to -2^63.
                        2              --Otherwise 2^<index> will fit fine.
                    )
                ), 
                N.[Number]-1 --We're using 1-based indexes, not 0-based, so the first bit needs to flip on 1, not 0.
            ) [IxBitmask]
    ) B
    WHERE N.[Number] <= LEN(@String2)
), cteCandidates AS (
    SELECT 
        S1.[Ix] [Ix1],
        S2.[Ix] [Ix2],
        S2.[IxBitMask],
        S1.[Chr]
    FROM cteStringVariables V
    CROSS JOIN cteString1 S1
    INNER JOIN cteString2 S2 ON S1.[Chr] = S2.[Chr] AND ABS(S1.[Ix] - S2.[Ix]) <= V.[Window]
), cteGreedy AS (
    --Anchor: Just the first matchable S1 character and its first match from S2
    SELECT TOP 1
        M.[Ix1],
        M.[Ix2],
        M.[IxBitMask] [Used], --Bit mask of which indexes from @String2 have been used. The first match is valid, so that's our starting mask.
        M.[Chr]
    FROM cteCandidates M
    ORDER BY M.[Ix1], M.[Ix2]
    UNION ALL
    --Recursive section: Each recursion selects the next match for an unused S1 and S2 character
    SELECT
        M.[Ix1],
        M.[Ix2],
        M.[IxBitmask]|G.[Used], --1s in the mask where either value has a 1
        M.[Chr]
    FROM cteGreedy G 
    --All matches for unused S1 and S2 characters, with a ROW_NUMBER() to allow us to pick the first one each time
    CROSS APPLY (
        SELECT
            M.[Ix1],
            M.[Ix2],
            M.[Chr],
            M.[IxBitmask],
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY M.[Ix1], M.[Ix2]) Rn --Will allow us to select only the first valid match
        FROM cteCandidates M
        WHERE M.[Ix1] > G.[Ix1]                --Ordering by Ix1 first means we can always move forwards through S1
            AND (M.[IxBitMask] & G.[Used]) = 0 --Checks if they have any bits in common. IxBitMask only has 1 bit flipped, so if they do, this Ix2 has been used.
    ) M
    WHERE M.[Rn] = 1 --Only add the first unused match in this recursion
), cteReIndexed AS (
    SELECT
        G.[Ix1],
        G.[Ix2],
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY G.[Ix1]) [O1],
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY G.[Ix2]) [O2],
        G.[Chr]
    FROM cteGreedy G
    WHERE [Ix1] IS NOT NULL
), cteMatches AS (
    SELECT 
        IIF(R1.[Chr]<>R2.[Chr],1,0) [IsTransposed]
    FROM cteReIndexed R1
    INNER JOIN cteReIndexed R2 ON R1.[O1] = R2.[O2]
), ctePrefix AS (
    --Winkler applies a bonus based on how many consecutive matches occur from the start of the up-to-4 character "prefix."
    --ctePrefix.Len gives us that number by finding the index (-1) of the first non-matching character pair in that prefix.
    SELECT 
        CASE
            WHEN M.[Ix] IS NOT NULL THEN M.[Ix]-1 --If any prefix characters mismatch, the earliest mismatch Index - 1
            WHEN V.[MinLen] > 3 THEN 4            --If both strings are longer than 3 characters and all prefix characters match, that's 4 characters
            ELSE V.[MinLen]                       --Otherwise the full length of the shortest string matches
        END [Len]
    FROM cteStringVariables V --single-row table to get the shortest string length from
    CROSS APPLY ( --CROSS APPLY so we don't kill that row if there are no matching characters
        SELECT MIN(S1.[Ix]) [Ix]
        FROM cteString1 S1
        INNER JOIN cteString2 S2 ON 
            S1.[Ix] = S2.[Ix]        --Match indexes of both strings
            AND S1.[Chr] <> S2.[Chr] --Only look for mismatched characters
        WHERE S1.[Ix] < 5            --Don't look beyond the 4-character prefix
    ) M
), cteJaroVariables AS (
    --For clarity, aggregate the variables that the Jaro portion will use into a single-row table
    SELECT
        COUNT(*) [m], --number of matching character pairs between the strings
        CAST(SUM(M.[IsTransposed]) AS float)/2 [t] --number of times 2 characters in a single string would need to be swapped to make the matches occur in the same order in both strings.
    FROM cteMatches M
)
SELECT
    --JaroWinklerScore will be NULL if we didn't generate any rows. Make it 1 if this is because we told it not to because the strings were a perfect match.
    IIF(@String1=@String2,1,W.[JaroWinklerScore]) [JaroWinklerScore]
FROM cteJaroVariables V
CROSS JOIN cteStringVariables S --We'll need to know the lengths of both strings (though it doesn't matter which is which)
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT
        (V.[m]/S.[MaxLen]) [MaxLenRatio],
        (V.[m]/S.[MinLen]) [MinLenRatio],
        (V.[m]-(V.[t]))/V.[m] [TranspositionModifier]
) R --For clarity, calculate the ratios used by Jaro first
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT (R.[MaxLenRatio]+R.[MinLenRatio]+R.[TranspositionModifier])/3 [JaroScore]
) J --Jaro score comes in here
CROSS JOIN ctePrefix P --We'll need to know the length of the matched prefix for Winkler
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT J.[JaroScore]+(P.[Len]*0.1*(1-J.[JaroScore])) [JaroWinklerScore]
) W --Apply Winkler bonus here
